prompt: Mist rolls in and you realise you might be lost. What does the US Forest Service tell you to do first?
options: Stop, stay calm and stay put
Walk quickly downhill to find a stream
Climb the nearest hill for a phone signal
Keep going the way you think the path runs
correctAnswer: Stop, stay calm and stay put
explanation: STOP begins with Stop: stay calm and stay put, because panic is your greatest enemy. Do not move until you have a specific reason to take a step.

prompt: People walk in circles when lost because one leg is longer or stronger than the other.
explanation: This is the myth. In the Max Planck study the same person veered left one time and right the next, so the cause is not a lopsided body. Small random errors in the senses add up and your sense of straight ahead drifts.

prompt: In the Max Planck experiments in the Sahara and a German forest, when did walkers manage to keep a straight path?
options: Only when the sun or moon was visible
Only when they were blindfolded
Only on cloudy days
Whenever they concentrated hard enough
correctAnswer: Only when the sun or moon was visible
explanation: Walkers held a straight course while they could see the sun or moon. As soon as the sun went behind cloud they began to circle without noticing.

prompt: Searchers move faster than you and work from your _____ known point, so every mile you wander makes their job harder.
explanation: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team explains that searchers start from your last known point; every mile you wander expands the search area enormously.

prompt: Match each step of STOP to what you do:

pairs.right: Stay calm and stay put until you have a reason to move
Go back over how you got here and what landmarks you should see
Get out your compass and work out directions
Weigh a few plans, then act on one

explanation: These are the US Forest Service steps. If you are not very, very confident of a route at the Plan stage, the answer is to stay put.

prompt: It is getting dark, you have twisted an ankle, and you think the car park is "probably" over the next ridge. What does the Forest Service advice say?
options: Stay where you are
Push for the ridge before it is fully dark
Follow the nearest stream downhill
Walk on a straight compass line until you hit a road
explanation: Nightfall, injury and exhaustion are each reasons to stay in place, and "probably" is not very, very confident.

prompt: A lost walker talks through their thinking. Which step is the mistake?
steps: I stop as soon as I suspect I am lost.
I go back over how I got here and which landmarks I should be able to see.
The map shows no stream here, so the map must be wrong; I carry on along this one.
If I am not very, very confident of a route, I stay put and make myself easy to find.
explanation: Step 3 is bending the map to fit. The rescue team rule is that the ground is right: stop and back up to the last point where you were certain.

prompt: Put these actions in a sensible order, from before the walk to waiting for rescue:
steps: Tell someone your route and when you will be back
Stop, stay calm and stay put
Think back over how you got here
Observe: get out your compass and check directions
Plan, staying put unless you are very, very confident
Hug a tree: stay by one fixed point and blow your whistle
explanation: Telling someone comes first, because staying put only works if a search is started. Then STOP in order, and finally stay with one fixed point and make noise.

prompt: You mark the tip of a stick's shadow, wait 15 minutes and mark the tip again. Which direction is the first mark?
options: West
East
North
South
explanation: The first shadow mark is always west, everywhere on Earth, because the sun crosses from east to west and the shadow moves the opposite way.

prompt: The sun always rises due east and sets due west.
explanation: This is the myth. The sun rises exactly east only around the equinoxes; the rest of the year the sunrise point slides along the horizon with the seasons.

prompt: You have joined your two shadow marks with a line. How do you face north?
options: Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right
Stand with the first mark on your right and the second on your left
Face along the shadow towards the stick
Face the sun at midday
correctAnswer: Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right
explanation: The first mark is west and the second east, so with west on your left you face north, in either hemisphere.

prompt: On the equinoxes, the tip of an upright stick's shadow follows a _____ path from west to east all day.
explanation: Only at the equinoxes does the shadow tip run in a straight line; on other days its path curves, which is why the quick method is approximate.

prompt: It is a winter afternoon in Scotland, with no summer time. You hold your watch flat and point the hour hand at the sun. Where is south?
options: Halfway between the hour hand and 12
Where the 12 points
Directly opposite the hour hand
Halfway between the hour hand and 6
correctAnswer: Halfway between the hour hand and 12
explanation: North of the equator, the line halfway between the hour hand and 12 runs north-south, with south on the side towards the sun at midday.

prompt: Match each situation to the right version of the watch trick:

pairs.right: Hour hand at the sun; halfway to 12 is south
Point 12 at the sun; take the midpoint to the hour hand
Use 1 instead of 12
Draw a clock face on paper with the correct time

explanation: All four come from the Army's watch method. Summer time shifts the sun's midday to 1 pm, so 1 replaces 12.

prompt: A friend explains the shadow-stick method. Which step is wrong?
steps: Push a straight stick about a metre long upright into level ground.
Mark the tip of the shadow; this first mark is always east.
Wait 10 to 15 minutes and mark the new tip.
Join the two marks for a rough east-west line.
Stand with the first mark on your left to face north.
explanation: The first mark is always west, not east. The shadow moves from west to east as the sun moves from east to west.

prompt: Why is the watch method less trustworthy near the equator than in Britain?
options: It treats the sun as turning evenly around you, and that gets worse the higher the sun climbs
Watches lose time in tropical heat
Near the equator the sun crosses the sky from west to east
Near the equator there are no shadows at all
correctAnswer: It treats the sun as turning evenly around you, and that gets worse the higher the sun climbs
explanation: The Army says the method is more accurate the further you are from the equator. Near the equator the sun climbs very high, so its compass direction does not turn evenly.

prompt: North of the equator, which star pattern has two "pointer" stars that lead you to Polaris?
options: The Plough (Big Dipper)
Orion's Belt
The Southern Cross
The Pleiades
explanation: The two stars on the outer lip of the Plough point to Polaris. Extend their line about five times the gap between them.

prompt: Polaris, the North Star, is the brightest star in the night sky.
explanation: This is the myth. People expect it to be very bright, but it is fairly ordinary. It is a supergiant, but 431 light years away, so it does not look very bright.

prompt: To reach Polaris, extend the line through the Plough's pointers about _____ times the gap between them.
explanation: The Army manual says about five times the distance between the pointer stars. Polaris sits on that line on its own.

prompt: You are camped in New Zealand and cannot see Polaris anywhere. What do you use to find south?
options: The Southern Cross and its pointer stars
The Plough's pointers
Cassiopeia's W
Whichever star is brightest overhead
correctAnswer: The Southern Cross and its pointer stars
explanation: There is no bright star near the south celestial pole, so you extend the Cross's long axis four and a half to five times and use the pointers to confirm.

prompt: Match each sky feature to its role:

pairs.right: Almost directly above the North Pole
Long axis leads towards the south pole of the sky
A W of five stars, roughly opposite the Plough
Dark patch between the Cross and its pointers

explanation: Polaris marks north; the Cross points to the south celestial pole; Cassiopeia helps when the Plough is low; the Coal Sack helps you tell the true Cross from the False Cross.

prompt: On the Hawaiian star compass, a navigator sees a star rise in a house in the north-east. Where will it set?
options: In the house of the same name in the north-west
Exactly due west
In the opposite house in the south-west
In the same house it rose in
correctAnswer: In the house of the same name in the north-west
explanation: A star rising in a north-eastern house sets in the same-named house on the north-western horizon, so each rising or setting star is a direction marker.

prompt: Marshallese stick charts were maps that navigators carried at sea to plot their course between islands.
explanation: This is the myth. Early scholars read them as charts, but later studies showed they were teaching devices showing how swells run, bend and cross. At sea, navigators felt the swells through the canoe.

prompt: Put the steps for finding true north at night in order:
steps: Find the Plough
Pick out the two pointer stars on the outer lip of the pan
Extend their line about five times their gap to Polaris
Drop an imaginary line from Polaris straight down to the horizon
Drive stakes pointing that way to travel by in daylight
explanation: Plough, pointers, Polaris, horizon, then stakes, so you can walk the line safely in the morning.

prompt: What is magnetic declination?
options: The angle between magnetic north and true north
The downward tilt of a compass needle
Your distance from the North Pole
The angle between grid north and the equator
correctAnswer: The angle between magnetic north and true north
explanation: Declination is the angle between magnetic north and true north, counted as east or west of true north.

prompt: A compass needle points straight at the geographic North Pole.
explanation: This is the myth. A needle lines up with the local magnetic field. Most of the time compasses do not point precisely towards the North Pole.

prompt: You have set a bearing on the compass dial. What does "red in the shed" mean?
options: Turn your whole body until the red needle lines up with the orienting arrow
Turn the dial until the red needle points at your destination
Point the red end at true north on the map
Keep the compass in a red case
correctAnswer: Turn your whole body until the red needle lines up with the orienting arrow
explanation: With the bearing set, you turn yourself, not the dial, until the needle sits in the orienting arrow; the direction-of-travel arrow then shows your way.

prompt: Around 60 CE the Han writer Wang Chong described a south-pointing _____ that came to rest pointing south when thrown on the ground.
explanation: The south-pointing spoon, made of lodestone and set on a bronze plate, is thought to be the ancestor of the compass.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning:

pairs.right: Towards the geographic North Pole
Where the grid lines on your map point
Where your compass needle points
The correction you apply between map and compass

explanation: Ordnance Survey's three norths, plus the grid magnetic angle printed on the map, which is correct only at the time of printing.

prompt: Walking in San Diego County, you forget the 11-degree declination. Roughly how far off course could you drift over a five-mile walk?
options: About a mile
About ten metres
About five miles
Not at all
explanation: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team warns of drifting about a mile for every five miles walked if you ignore the declination there.

prompt: Which step in taking a bearing is the mistake?
steps: Lay the compass edge from where you are to where you are going, with the direction-of-travel arrow towards the destination.
Turn the dial until the orienting lines match the map's north-south grid lines.
Apply the grid magnetic angle printed on the map.
Hold the compass right beside your phone so the screen lights up the needle.
Turn your whole body until the red needle sits in the orienting arrow, then walk to a landmark.
explanation: Phones, magnetic buttons and metal belts can deflect the needle. Keep the compass away from them.

prompt: Why did compasses at Greenwich point to true north in September 2019?
options: The line of zero declination, moving west at about 20 km a year, crossed Greenwich
The geographic North Pole shifted towards London
The Royal Observatory recalibrated every compass on the site
The railways near Greenwich stopped running on electricity
correctAnswer: The line of zero declination, moving west at about 20 km a year, crossed Greenwich
explanation: Declination changes as Earth's field changes. The agonic line reached Greenwich in 2019 for the first time in about 360 years.

prompt: In the ground-to-air emergency code, what does a large V laid out on the ground mean?
options: Require assistance
Require medical assistance
Yes
Proceed in this direction
explanation: V means require assistance, X require medical assistance, N no, Y yes, and an arrow proceed in this direction.

prompt: Moss grows only on the north side of trees, so it makes a reliable compass.
explanation: This is the myth. Moss grows wherever it is shady and moist, sometimes all the way round a trunk. North of the equator it is most likely on the north side, but not exclusively.

prompt: You are hurt on a hillside in Wales and have a whistle. What signal does Mountain Rescue England and Wales ask for?
options: Six long blasts in a minute, a minute's pause, then repeat
One long blast every hour
Three blasts, then stop once you hear a reply
Blow continuously until you are out of breath
correctAnswer: Six long blasts in a minute, a minute's pause, then repeat
explanation: Six good long blasts in a minute, stop for a minute, repeat, and do not stop because you hear a reply: your blasts may guide the team in.

prompt: Each ground-to-air symbol should be at least 4 m wide and _____ m long.
explanation: The Army asks for symbols at least 4 m wide and 6 m long, with arms 1 m wide, in materials that contrast with the ground.

prompt: North of the equator, match each clue to what it tells you:

pairs.right: Cooler and damper, with lingering snow
Among the first places to lose snow in winter
Points about 28 degrees east of south
A linear feature where lost people are often found

explanation: The slope and snow clues come from the sun standing in the south. Dishes aim at satellites east of south, and Koester finds most lost people close to linear features.

prompt: It is night and you want to signal distress with fire. What is the international distress signal?
options: Three fires in a triangle about 25 m apart
One huge bonfire
Two fires side by side
A single fire ringed with stones
correctAnswer: Three fires in a triangle about 25 m apart
explanation: Three fires in a triangle, or in a line about 25 m apart, is the international distress signal; by day, three columns of smoke.

prompt: A survivor plans a mirror signal. Which step is the mistake?
steps: Get to the highest clear ground you can reach.
Catch the sun's glare on your palm.
Hold up two fingers in a V with the aircraft between them.
Flash the beam rapidly and hold it on the cockpit for as long as possible.
Rock the mirror slowly off your hand and onto the aircraft.
explanation: Never flash rapidly, and do not hold the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds, as it may blind the pilot.

prompt: A felled conifer's rings are much wider on one side. What is the most careful way to read it?
options: The tree may have been tilted and built compression wood on its underside, so it is not a reliable compass
The wide side always faces the equator
The wide side always faces north
The tree must have grown in the Southern Hemisphere
correctAnswer: The tree may have been tilted and built compression wood on its underside, so it is not a reliable compass
explanation: Sources disagree: the Army manuals say rings are wider towards the equator, but WSL tree-ring scientists show wide rings on one side record a tilt, with compression wood on the underside.
